spec.title: Password Reset
spec.summary: Behavior a correct, enumeration-resistant password-reset flow must implement: token generation and lifecycle, response consistency, throttling, completion semantics, and post-reset state.
applies_when: Public users or existing accounts can request a password reset.
The application authenticates users with passwords it controls.
does_not_apply_when: Authentication is entirely delegated to an external identity provider that owns the reset flow.
The application has no passwords (e.g., passkeys/magic-link only) — parts of this spec still apply to equivalent recovery flows.

rules.title: Reset flows must not reveal whether an account exists
rules.statement: The externally observable result of requesting a password reset — message, status code, and response timing — must be equivalent whether or not the supplied account exists.
why: Reset endpoints are the easiest enumeration oracle in most applications.
OWASP requires a consistent message for existent and non-existent accounts, uniform response time, and no behavior differences that allow account discovery.
ASVS extends the same protection to registration and forgot-password flows (V6 6.3.8).
applies_when: The reset-request endpoint is reachable by unauthenticated users.
failure_modes: A "reset link sent" message for real accounts versus a "no such user" error otherwise.
Different HTTP status codes (200 vs 404) between the two cases.
Response-time differences (hashing/verification runs only for existing accounts).
Rate limiting applied only to known accounts, revealing them through throttling.

evidence.locator: Introduction; Forgot Password Request
evidence.note: Requires a consistent message for existent and non-existent accounts and uniform response time, without behavior differences that allow account discovery; Boring scopes this to unauthenticated reset-request endpoints.

evidence.locator: Authentication and Error Messages — Authentication Responses; Password recovery examples; Error Codes and URLs
evidence.note: Requires a generic recovery response regardless of account existence or lock state, with the correct example "If that email address is in our database..."; HTTP status codes must not differ even when the displayed message is generic.
Registration and forgot-password flows must not allow deducing valid users from error messages, HTTP response codes, or response-time differences.

scenarios.given: an existing account and a non-existent account
scenarios.when: a password reset is requested for each
expect: responses are indistinguishable in message, status code, and response-time distribution

scenarios.given: a deleted or deactivated account
scenarios.when: a password reset is requested
expect: the response is equivalent to the non-existent-account case

rules.title: Reset tokens must be unguessable
rules.statement: Reset tokens must be generated with a cryptographically secure random generator and be sufficiently long to resist guessing under the application's threat model.
why: A guessable token converts the reset flow into an account takeover primitive.
OWASP requires tokens to be randomly generated using a cryptographically safe algorithm and long enough to protect against brute-force attacks; it does not set one universal entropy threshold here.
Sequential, timestamp-based, or hashed-known-data tokens are predictable in practice.
applies_when: Any reset token, code, or link capability is issued.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Tokens derived from user ID plus a timestamp or MAC.
Short numeric codes reused from other flows without adjusted entropy.
Tokens generated with non-cryptographic randomness (Math.random-style PRNGs).

evidence.locator: Introduction; General Security Practices
evidence.note: Requires tokens to be randomly generated with a cryptographically safe algorithm and long enough to resist brute force; Boring requires a CSPRNG and threat-model-justified strength without prescribing one universal entropy number.

scenarios.given: many reset tokens issued for many accounts
scenarios.when: the token corpus is examined
expect: tokens show no structure, sequence, or cross-account predictability
generation traces to a CSPRNG and the chosen strength is justified by the application's threat model

rules.title: Reset tokens must expire
rules.statement: Reset tokens must have a bounded lifetime and be rejected after that lifetime.
why: A reset token is a temporary credential; an unbounded one is a permanent backdoor, especially once it leaks (email forwarding, logs, device sync).
OWASP requires tokens to expire after an appropriate period; the appropriate bound depends on the recovery channel and threat model.
applies_when: Any reset token or code is issued.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Tokens valid indefinitely or for weeks.
Expiry checked at request time rather than at completion time.

evidence.locator: Introduction
evidence.note: Introduction requires tokens to "expire after an appropriate period"; Boring requires a bounded, documented lifetime rejected at completion time, with the bound chosen for the recovery channel and threat model.

scenarios.given: a reset token issued more than the configured lifetime ago
scenarios.when: it is submitted to the completion endpoint
expect: the token is rejected and no credential change occurs

rules.title: Reset tokens must be single-use
rules.statement: A reset token must be invalidated by its successful use. Submitting the same token again must be rejected, including when submissions race.
why: A reusable token that leaks is a repeated-takeover key for the lifetime of the token.
OWASP requires tokens to be single use and invalidated after use.
applies_when: Any reset token or code is issued.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: The token remains valid after completion (replay weeks later).
Two concurrent completions with the same token both succeed.

evidence.locator: Introduction; General Security Practices — Invalidated after they have been used
evidence.note: Requires tokens to be single-use and invalidated after use; Boring enforces this under concurrency, so at most one of two simultaneous completions takes effect.

scenarios.given: a reset token that has already completed a password change
scenarios.when: the same token is submitted again
expect: the password is not changed and the token is rejected

scenarios.given: two completion requests carrying the same valid token
scenarios.when: they are processed simultaneously
expect: at most one changes the password; the other is rejected or made ineffective

rules.title: The account must not be modified until a valid token is presented
rules.statement: Validation happens at completion: the token must be verified — existence, expiry, use state, account binding — at the moment the credential changes, and the account must not be modified before that.
why: Pre-authorizing an account at request time (e.g., marking it reset-pending and trusting that flag) turns any completion-path bug into account takeover.
OWASP requires that no change be made to the account until a valid token is presented.
applies_when: Reset completion changes credentials or account state.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: The request step flips a "reset approved" flag that the completion step trusts without validating the token again.
Expiry or use state checked only on the first request, not on the mutating call.

evidence.locator: Introduction — Do not make a change to the account until a valid token is presented
evidence.note: Prohibits any account change, including lockout, before a valid token is presented; Boring applies this at the mutating completion step, re-checking existence, expiry, use state, and account binding.

scenarios.given: an account with a reset request in flight whose token has since expired or been used
scenarios.when: the completion endpoint is called with that token
expect: no credential or account state change occurs

rules.title: Reset completion must be bound to the token's account
rules.statement: The password changed is the one belonging to the account the token was issued for. Client-supplied identifiers (user ID, email in the form) must not be able to redirect the change to a different account.
why: Tokens are issued for one account; letting the client name the target account is a mass-assignment bug that enables takeover of any account whose reset link was obtained.
OWASP requires tokens to be linked to an individual user in the database.
applies_when: Reset completion accepts any client-supplied identifier alongside the token.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: The completion form includes an email/user field that overrides token-derived identity.
Token lookup keys on a client-supplied email, so one valid token resets whichever account that email names.

evidence.locator: General Security Practices — Linked to an individual user in the database
evidence.note: Requires each token to resolve to the individual user it was issued for; Boring prohibits client-supplied identifiers from redirecting the credential change to another account.

scenarios.given: a valid reset token for account A
scenarios.when: the completion request claims account B (different email or user ID)
expect: account B's password is unchanged and the request is rejected

rules.title: Reset endpoints must be throttled without enabling enumeration
rules.statement: Reset request and completion endpoints should use abuse controls such as rate limiting, per-account and per-source where appropriate, while keeping responses indistinguishable between known and unknown accounts and avoiding account lockout from reset-request floods.
why: Without throttling, the endpoint becomes an email-bombing tool and a token brute-force surface.
OWASP recommends per-account rate limiting and other controls, and explicitly warns that accounts should not be locked out in response to a forgotten-password attack.
NIST requires rate limiting for specified authentication events; that supports the control but does not prescribe one universal reset-endpoint algorithm.
applies_when: Reset request or completion is reachable by unauthenticated users.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Throttling applied only for existing accounts, leaking account existence (conflicts with BORING-AUTH-RESET-001).
Reset floods lock accounts, producing a denial-of-service on login.

evidence.locator: Forgot Password Request — per-account rate limiting / CAPTCHA; URL Tokens — rate limiting token brute force; Account Lockout
evidence.note: Requires abuse controls such as per-account rate limiting or CAPTCHA against inbox flooding and token guessing, while warning that accounts must not be locked out by a forgotten-password attack.

evidence.locator: Rate limiting for authentication failures (throttling guidance)
evidence.note: NIST requires rate limiting for authentication events generally; Boring derives the reset-specific application — throttle request and completion without distinguishing known from unknown accounts and without causing lockout — since neither source prescribes one universal reset algorithm.

scenarios.given: many reset requests from one source, for a mix of existing and non-existing accounts
scenarios.when: the responses are compared
expect: throttling engages without making account existence distinguishable
no account becomes un-loginable because of the flood

rules.title: The new password must satisfy the same policy as normal credential creation
rules.statement: Completing a reset should enforce the same password policy as normal credential creation, including the application's documented length and compromised-password rules.
why: Reset completion is password creation; weakening the policy there reopens the weakest door.
OWASP requires the same password policy used elsewhere in the application to apply on reset.
NIST requires a minimum length (15 characters single-factor, 8 with MFA) and SHALL-level blocklist comparison against breached passwords; composition rules must not be imposed.
applies_when: Reset completion sets a new password.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Reset accepts a one-character password that registration would reject.
Breached-password checks skipped because "the user proved identity via email".

evidence.locator: User Resets Password; URL Tokens; PINs — same password policy as elsewhere in the application
evidence.note: Requires the application's existing password policy to be applied at reset completion, including the confirm-twice step; Boring treats reset as password creation with no weakened emergency variant.

evidence.locator: Password verifiers — minimum length (15 single-factor / 8 with MFA), SHOULD allow 64+, SHALL blocklist breached passwords, SHALL NOT impose composition rules
evidence.note: Establishes the modern policy baseline Boring references — length plus breach blocklist, no composition rules; the rule still defers to the application's documented policy rather than fixing one universal threshold.

scenarios.given: the application's password policy
scenarios.when: a reset completes with a password that violates it
expect: the reset is rejected with the same feedback registration would produce

rules.title: Completing a reset must end existing sessions
rules.statement: After a password reset completes, previously established sessions should be invalidated automatically or by an explicit user choice. The flow should not silently log the user in as a side effect of recovery.
why: Sessions established before the reset may belong to whoever had the old credential; keeping them alive defeats the point of the reset.
OWASP requires offering the user invalidation of all existing sessions (or invalidating automatically), and not logging the user in automatically after reset.
ASVS requires the option to terminate all other active sessions after a change or removal of an authentication factor (V7 7.4.3).
applies_when: The application has cookie- or token-based sessions.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: The attacker's session survives the victim's reset.
Reset auto-logs-in the person holding the token — different person than the account owner when a link was intercepted.

evidence.locator: User Resets Password — ask to invalidate all existing sessions or invalidate automatically; do not log the user in automatically
evidence.note: Requires offering or performing session invalidation after reset and prohibits automatic login, since the token holder is not always the account owner.

evidence.locator: V7.4 Session Termination (7.4.3: option to terminate all other active sessions after a credential change)
evidence.note: Requires the ability to terminate other active sessions after an authentication-factor change; Boring applies this to the post-reset flow with an explicit-preserve opt-out.

scenarios.given: an account with an active session and a completed password reset
scenarios.when: the old session is used after the reset
expect: the old session is rejected (or was explicitly preserved by the user's documented choice)

rules.title: Notify the account owner when the password changes
rules.statement: A notification that the password was changed should be sent to the account's address of record — without including the new password, the token, or a working reset link.
why: The notification is the victim's detection signal for an in-progress takeover.
OWASP requires informing the user that their password was reset and warns never to send the password in that email.
ASVS requires user notification after updates to authentication details such as credential resets (V6 6.3.7).
applies_when: Reset completion changes a credential.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: The confirmation email contains a "click here to set a new password" link with a fresh token — a second takeover key.
The email includes the new password in plaintext.

evidence.locator: User Resets Password — send an email informing the user the password was reset; do not send the password in the email
evidence.note: Requires a post-reset notification to the user without including the password; Boring extends the inert-notification requirement to tokens and working reset links, which would otherwise be a second takeover key.
Requires notifying users after credential resets or username/email changes; Boring scopes this to the address of record held before the reset.

scenarios.given: a completed password reset
scenarios.when: notifications are inspected
expect: the account's address of record received a change notification
the notification contains no token, no reset link, and no password

rules.title: Reset-token values at rest must not be recoverable
rules.statement: Stored reset-token data should not allow recovery of a working token after a read-only breach: keep only a non-recoverable representation (for example a hash verified by comparison on presentation) or in equivalently protected secret infrastructure, with each token bound to exactly one account. Short single-factor codes need a slow, salted hash and throttling because their entropy is low; high-entropy tokens still must not sit in plaintext columns, backups, or logs.
why: A database dump containing live reset tokens converts a data breach into immediate account takeover, before users rotate anything.

OWASP requires tokens to be stored securely as discussed in the Password Storage Cheat Sheet, and linked to an individual user; the Password Storage sheet describes salted, slow hashing with work factors as the reference mechanism.

The exact hash construction is an implementation choice for the token's entropy and threat model, which is why this stays SHOULD with an equivalent-protection exception rather than mandating one KDF for every token type.
applies_when: Reset tokens are persisted.
exceptions: Systems storing tokens in dedicated secret infrastructure with equivalent protection.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Plaintext token columns in the users table.
Tokens stored in logs, analytics events, or cache dumps.

evidence.locator: Introduction — Stored securely; General Security Practices — Stored in a secure manner, as discussed in the Password Storage Cheat Sheet; Linked to an individual user in the database
evidence.note: Directly requires secure storage per the Password Storage guidance plus per-user linkage; Boring interprets "securely" as non-recoverable at rest with per-account binding, not as any specific hash algorithm.

evidence.locator: Password Storage — salted, slow hashing (Argon2id, bcrypt, PBKDF2) with work factors; salt and hash stored per credential
evidence.note: Provides the reference hashing construction Boring derives token storage from; applied to tokens as a derived interpretation since the sheet targets passwords and Boring allows equivalent secret infrastructure and entropy-appropriate construction.

scenarios.given: the token persistence layer
scenarios.when: its contents are inspected
expect: no plaintext reset tokens are recoverable from the database, backups, or logs

rules.title: Treat reset links as secrets during transport
rules.statement: Deliberately decide how the token reaches the user and minimize its exposure: links pasted into emails leak through browser history, server and proxy logs, Referer headers, link previews, and analytics — design so those channels do not silently keep a working credential.
why: The token is a bearer credential; every system that sees the URL sees the credential.
URL-referenced secrets leak through Referer headers to third-party resources, a failure mode well documented for session identifiers.
The trade-offs (link convenience versus token pasting) differ per product, which is why this is CONSIDER rather than MUST.
applies_when: Reset tokens are delivered via clickable links.
failure_modes: Full reset URLs (with token) in server logs, APM traces, or analytics pageviews.
Email link previews and mail-client scanners consuming the single-use token before the user clicks.
Third-party assets on the reset page receiving the token via Referer.

evidence.locator: Session Management Implementation — IDs in URLs disclose via links, logs, browser history, bookmarks, Referer header, search engines; Logging — do not include session IDs in logs, log a salted hash instead
evidence.note: Documents the URL-secret leakage channels for session identifiers; Boring derives the same treatment for reset tokens in links since a reset URL is likewise a bearer credential, while the delivery decision itself stays product-specific (CONSIDER).

evidence.locator: URL Tokens — HTTPS reset URLs; Referrer-Policy noreferrer to avoid referrer leakage
evidence.note: Directly requires HTTPS reset URLs and a noreferrer Referrer Policy on the reset page; Boring generalizes to auditing all retention channels (logs, analytics, previews) for still-valid tokens.

scenarios.given: a completed reset flow
scenarios.when: logs, analytics events, and outbound requests from the reset page are inspected
expect: no channel retains a still-valid token

rules.title: Define the policy for multiple outstanding reset requests
rules.statement: Decide and document what happens when a reset is requested while another token is outstanding: strong default is newest-wins (issuing a new token invalidates previous ones), but the essential requirement is that the behavior is defined, enforced, and enumeration-safe.
why: Every outstanding token is a live credential; unbounded accumulation multiplies exposure.
The correct product behavior varies (self-service vs support-driven flows), so this is a decision to make deliberately, not a universal constant.
applies_when: Repeated reset requests for the same account are possible (always).
failure_modes: Every request mints an independently valid token; ten requests leave ten working keys.
Only the newest token works, but older ones remain in the database long past their usefulness.

evidence.locator: Introduction; General Security Practices — single-use and invalidation
evidence.note: OWASP requires single-use invalidation but defines no outstanding-token policy; Boring derives the bounded-exposure default (newest-wins) as an operational interpretation, with the enforceable requirement being a documented, enumeration-safe policy.

scenarios.given: two reset requests issued in sequence for the same account
scenarios.when: each token is submitted after the second request
expect: behavior matches the documented policy (e.g., only the newest token is accepted)

rules.title: Post-reset redirects must not be attacker-controlled
rules.statement: The redirect target after a completed reset should be fixed or validated against an allowlist — a client-supplied redirect parameter must not be able to send the user to an external site.
why: Reset pages are prime open-redirect targets because the victim arrives trusting the flow ("your password was changed, continue…").
Unvalidated redirects are a well-established web vulnerability class covered by the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide.
applies_when: The reset flow redirects after completion or request.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: A ?next=https://evil.example parameter carries the freshly-reset, now-logged-out user to a phishing page.
Protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.example`) bypass a host-suffix check.

evidence.locator: Testing for Client-side URL Redirect (WSTG-CLNT-04)
evidence.note: Covers open redirection where user-controlled input selects an external target for phishing; Boring applies this to the post-reset redirect parameter with an allowlist or fixed-target requirement.

scenarios.given: a completion request carrying a redirect parameter pointing off-site
scenarios.when: the reset completes
expect: the redirect stays within the application (allowlisted target or default page)

spec.title: Sessions
spec.summary: Behavior a correct session-management implementation must implement: identifier generation, lifecycle (login, logout, timeout, credential change, privilege change), cookie hardening, and token-based sessions.
applies_when: The application maintains authenticated state across requests for users.
does_not_apply_when: The application is fully stateless per request (e.g., pure APIs authenticating every call) — rules about token-based sessions still apply where they are used.

rules.title: Session identifiers must be unguessable and carry no meaning
rules.statement: Session identifiers must be generated with a cryptographically secure random generator, be sufficiently unpredictable for the application's threat model, and contain no user, role, or other meaningful data.
why: Predictable session IDs let an attacker obtain valid sessions for other users.
OWASP requires strong entropy from a CSPRNG; its numeric guidance is a baseline for session identifiers, not a universal substitute for threat-model analysis.
Embedding PII or role data in the identifier leaks information wherever the identifier is logged or observed.
applies_when: Any server-issued session, cookie, or bearer identifier.
failure_modes: Sequential or timestamp-based session IDs.
Identifiers encoding username or role, or generated with a non-cryptographic PRNG.

evidence.locator: Session ID Properties; Cookies; Session ID Life Cycle; Session Expiration
evidence.note: The cited OWASP-SESSION-MANAGEMENT section directly supports this behavior; Boring narrows it to the applicability conditions recorded above.

scenarios.given: many session identifiers collected over time and across users
scenarios.when: the corpus is examined
expect: no structure, sequence, or cross-user predictability

rules.title: Regenerate the session identifier at authentication and privilege changes
rules.statement: The session identifier must be regenerated during login — replacing any pre-authentication identifier — and again after any privilege level change.
why: Regeneration at login is the standard defense against session fixation — an attacker who planted a known identifier gains nothing when it is replaced.
OWASP makes regeneration mandatory during authentication and after any privilege-level change.
applies_when: Sessions are established or elevated server-side.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Login keeps the attacker-chosen session ID (fixation).
A user promoted to admin keeps the identifier issued to their low-privilege session.

evidence.locator: Session ID Properties; Cookies; Session ID Life Cycle; Session Expiration
evidence.note: The cited OWASP-SESSION-MANAGEMENT section directly supports this behavior; Boring narrows it to the applicability conditions recorded above.

scenarios.given: a client holding a pre-authentication session identifier
scenarios.when: the client logs in
expect: the authenticated session uses a freshly generated identifier

scenarios.given: an authenticated user whose privilege level changes
scenarios.when: the privilege change is applied
expect: the session identifier is regenerated

rules.title: Logout must invalidate the session server-side
rules.statement: Logout must destroy the session's server-side state (or, for self-contained tokens, revoke via key/allowlist mechanisms) — clearing the client cookie alone is not logout.
why: A cookie cleared client-side leaves the token valid; anyone who copied it continues to act as the user.
OWASP requires the application to invalidate the session at least on the server side; ASVS requires the same for logout (V7 7.4.1).
applies_when: Any session termination, user-initiated or system-initiated.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Logout only deletes the cookie; the stolen session still works.
A "logout everywhere" feature that clears cookies for all devices without invalidating any server-side session.

evidence.locator: Session ID Properties; Cookies; Session ID Life Cycle; Session Expiration
evidence.note: The cited OWASP-SESSION-MANAGEMENT section directly supports this behavior; Boring narrows it to the applicability conditions recorded above.

scenarios.given: a captured copy of the session token
scenarios.when: the user logs out and the captured token is replayed
expect: the server rejects the token

rules.title: Sessions must have enforced idle and absolute timeouts
rules.statement: Sessions must expire after a period of inactivity and after a maximum absolute lifetime, enforced server-side. The application must select and document bounds based on risk, session purpose, and operational constraints.
why: Without timeouts, a stolen session or an abandoned kiosk login is valid forever.
OWASP gives concrete ranges, idle timeouts of 2–5 minutes for high-value applications and 15–30 minutes for low-risk, with 4–8 hours as an appropriate absolute timeout range.
ASVS requires inactivity and absolute timeouts sized by documented risk analysis (V7 7.3.1/7.3.2).
applies_when: Any session with a lifetime beyond a single request.
exceptions: Deliberate long-lived sessions (e.g., refresh-token models) must document the risk decision and compensate with rotation and revocation.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Sessions that never expire; "remember me" implemented by removing expiry entirely.
Timeouts enforced only client-side.

evidence.locator: Session ID Properties; Cookies; Session ID Life Cycle; Session Expiration
evidence.note: The cited OWASP-SESSION-MANAGEMENT section directly supports this behavior; Boring narrows it to the applicability conditions recorded above.

scenarios.given: an idle session and a session beyond its absolute lifetime
scenarios.when: each is used
expect: both are rejected server-side

rules.title: Cookie-based sessions must set Secure and HttpOnly
rules.statement: Session cookies must be marked Secure and HttpOnly: Secure prevents the identifier from crossing cleartext connections; HttpOnly blocks its theft by scripts after XSS.
why: OWASP marks both attributes as mandatory for session cookies.
Without HttpOnly, every XSS becomes a session-hijacking vector; without Secure, one network downgrade leaks the identifier.
applies_when: Session identifiers are stored in cookies.
does_not_apply_when: Sessions are carried by bearer tokens outside cookies.
failure_modes: Session cookie without HttpOnly reachable from injected scripts.
Secure omitted so the cookie rides on http:// or is stripped on the HTTPS redirect.

evidence.locator: Session ID Properties; Cookies; Session ID Life Cycle; Session Expiration
evidence.note: The cited OWASP-SESSION-MANAGEMENT section directly supports this behavior; Boring narrows it to the applicability conditions recorded above.

scenarios.given: a Set-Cookie response establishing a session
scenarios.when: its attributes are inspected
expect: Secure and HttpOnly are present

rules.title: Cookie-based sessions must set a SameSite policy
rules.statement: Session cookies must set SameSite=Strict (preferred) or SameSite=Lax; SameSite=None must never be used without Secure.
why: SameSite is the browser's cross-site request boundary; without it, session cookies ride on cross-site forged requests.
OWASP requires an explicit SameSite policy (Strict preferred) and forbids None without Secure.
SameSite complements but does not replace CSRF defenses (OWASP CSRF Cheat Sheet).
applies_when: Session identifiers are stored in cookies.
does_not_apply_when: Sessions are carried by bearer tokens outside cookies.
failure_modes: No SameSite attribute, falling back to browser defaults that differ per browser and version.
SameSite=None without Secure, which browsers reject or expose.

evidence.locator: Session ID Properties; Cookies; Session ID Life Cycle; Session Expiration
evidence.note: The cited OWASP-SESSION-MANAGEMENT section directly supports this behavior; Boring narrows it to the applicability conditions recorded above.

scenarios.given: a Set-Cookie response establishing a session
scenarios.when: its attributes are inspected
expect: an explicit SameSite policy of Strict or Lax is present

rules.title: Credential changes must invalidate existing sessions
rules.statement: After a password change or reset, all sessions established before the change must be invalidated — automatically or by explicit user choice — so that a credential theft ends when the credential does.
why: The most common reason to change a password is suspicion that someone else has it; keeping their sessions alive defeats the action.
OWASP requires regeneration/invalidation after password changes; ASVS requires the option to terminate all other sessions after any change or removal of an authentication factor (V7 7.4.3).
applies_when: Passwords are changed or reset through any flow.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: The attacker's session survives the victim's password change.
Reset completes without touching the session store.

evidence.locator: Session ID Properties; Cookies; Session ID Life Cycle; Session Expiration
evidence.note: The cited OWASP-SESSION-MANAGEMENT section directly supports this behavior; Boring narrows it to the applicability conditions recorded above.

scenarios.given: sessions from before a password change
scenarios.when: they are used after the change
expect: they are rejected (or were explicitly preserved by the user's documented choice)

rules.title: Privilege changes must take effect in active sessions
rules.statement: Authorization changes — role changes, permission revocations, account disabling or deletion — must be reflected in already-active sessions within a bounded, documented window: by regenerating/refreshing the session, re-evaluating permissions per request, or terminating the session.
why: A demoted admin or revoked employee must not keep working through an existing session.
OWASP requires session renewal after any privilege-level change; ASVS requires terminating sessions when accounts are disabled or deleted (V7 7.4.2).
applies_when: Authorization state can change while sessions are active.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Permissions read once at login and cached for the session lifetime.

rules.statement: Right-to-left and bidirectional text must be stored intact (not stripped or reordered) and rendered within directional isolates, so mixed- direction content displays correctly and cannot visually reorder adjacent application UI or logs.
why: Stripping bidi controls corrupts names and addresses written in RTL scripts; displaying user text without isolation lets bidi overrides reorganize surrounding UI text (a spoofing vector known as Trojan Source in code, and log-reordering in terminals).
The Unicode Bidi Algorithm defines how mixed-direction text is ordered; isolates are its mechanism for scoping the effect.

rules.statement: When text is compared case-insensitively (emails, usernames, search), comparison should use Unicode case folding; locale-sensitive casing (notably Turkish I) must be applied only where locale is known and the semantics are truly locale-specific.
why: Methods like toLowerCase() and toUpperCase() are locale-dependent transformations; the dotless-İ mapping makes naive comparisons wrong for Turkish text.
Case folding is Unicode's defined mechanism for caseless matching (The Unicode Standard, casefold mappings).

rules.statement: Numeric and temporal text should be parsed with explicit, tested grammars — deciding leading zeros, plus signs, whitespace, locale separators, exponent notation — rather than loose or homemade patterns; rejected forms should fail with clear errors.
why: Forms like 010, +42, 1e5, 1.234,56, and " 42 " are accepted by some parsers and rejected by others; the ambiguity becomes corrupted amounts and off-by-1000 errors.
Locale conventions (decimal comma vs point, thousand separators) are defined in CLDR; parsing them requires deliberate choices, not assumptions.

rules.statement: Email addresses, URLs, and similar structured identifiers should be parsed and validated with maintained implementations of their specifications — not with homemade regexes; where specifications conflict, the application should choose and document one deliberately.
why: Email syntax alone spans RFC 5321/5322 (dot-atoms, quoted local parts), internationalized addresses (RFC 6531 SMTPUTF8), and IDNA domains (RFC 5890, UTS
Homemade regexes routinely reject valid addresses and accept malformed ones; the cost of a false rejection (locked-out user) exceeds the cost of accepting a syntactically-odd-but-deliverable address.

spec.title: Pagination
spec.summary: Behavior a correct paginated list must implement: a stable total order, duplicate- and skip-free traversal under concurrent writes, opaque and query-bound cursors, truthful end-of-list signals, enforced page-size bounds, correct backward traversal, and deliberate totals and cursor-lifetime policies. Framework-neutral; ordinary data correctness, not access control.
applies_when: The application exposes an ordered list that clients fetch in pages across multiple requests (REST, GraphQL, or database-backed listing).
does_not_apply_when: The entire result set is always returned in a single response with no paging parameters.
Pagination is purely presentational over a fixed, immutable in-memory array that never changes between requests (ordering rules still apply if the array can change).

rules.title: Order paged results by a stable total order
rules.statement: Paged results must be ordered by an explicit sort whose keys, taken together, uniquely identify each row — including a unique tiebreaker (typically the primary key) whenever the business sort key can tie.
why: Without a unique order, page boundaries cut through an undefined sequence and identical requests return different pages.
Tying sort values (same timestamp, same priority, same name) are the common case, not the exception; the tiebreaker is what makes positions stable.
SQL guarantees no order without ORDER BY, and different LIMIT/OFFSET subsets then give inconsistent results.
applies_when: Any paginated query exists.
failure_modes: Paging by created_at alone while hundreds of rows share one timestamp; tied rows duplicate and vanish across pages.
No ORDER BY at all; two identical page-1 requests return different items.
Tiebreaker sorted in a different direction than the business key, silently breaking tuple comparison.

evidence.locator: §7.6 LIMIT and OFFSET — ORDER BY must constrain rows into a unique order; §7.5 Sorting Rows — order guaranteed only when explicitly chosen
evidence.note: Directly requires a unique-constraining ORDER BY and warns that different LIMIT/OFFSET values otherwise give inconsistent, unpredictable subsets; Boring applies this to every paged API as a total order with tiebreaker.

scenarios.given: a dataset with many rows sharing one sort-key value
scenarios.when: all pages are fetched at a fixed page size
expect: every row appears exactly once across the full traversal
repeating the traversal returns the same row-to-page assignment

rules.title: Keep traversal stable when rows are inserted or deleted between pages
rules.statement: Traversal across pages should not duplicate or skip items when rows are inserted or deleted mid-traversal. The strong default for changing datasets is a position-anchored (keyset/cursor) continuation rather than a row-offset skip; offset paging remains acceptable where the dataset is small, effectively static, or random access matters more than shift-stability, provided the tradeoff is documented.
why: Offsets name a position ("skip 20"), so any insert or delete ahead of the window shifts every later page.
Keyset continuations name a place in the sort order ("after this key"), so other rows' inserts and deletes do not move the resume point.
Feeds, timelines, and large tables change during traversal in practice; admin lists of a dozen static rows do not, which is why this is SHOULD, not MUST.
applies_when: Clients traverse more than one page while the underlying dataset can change.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: New rows at the head duplicate the boundary rows onto the next offset page.
Deleted rows in an early page silently skip the rows that slid forward.

evidence.locator: §7.6 — different LIMIT/OFFSET subsets give inconsistent results without predictable ordering
evidence.note: Directly establishes offset instability; Boring scopes the SHOULD to changing multi-page traversals and names keyset continuation as the strong default.

evidence.locator: Cursor pagination via starting_after / ending_before object-ID cursors
evidence.note: Stripe's cursor design is derived here as the position-anchored pattern: resuming after an object ID rather than skipping N rows.

evidence.locator: LastEvaluatedKey / ExclusiveStartKey keyset resumption
evidence.note: DynamoDB's keyset resumption is derived as the same pattern at the storage layer: the continuation is the last evaluated key, not a row count.

scenarios.given: a traversal in progress at page 2 of a changing feed
scenarios.when: rows are inserted at the head and deleted from earlier pages before the next fetch
expect: no row appears twice and no row is silently skipped (within the documented concurrent-change policy)

rules.title: Treat cursors as opaque, untrusted input
rules.statement: Cursors must be treated as opaque client round-trips and validated on receipt. Malformed, forged, foreign, or expired cursors must be rejected with a clear error or handled per documented policy — never crash the server, leak internals, or return another scope's data.
why: Cursors arrive from the network; hand-edited, truncated, replayed, or cross-endpoint cursors are normal traffic, not edge fantasies.
Decoding a cursor without validation turns pagination into an injection and information-disclosure surface.
Opaque means the client must not need to understand cursor internals to page correctly.
applies_when: The API accepts client-supplied cursors or page tokens.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: A truncated base64 cursor raises an unhandled exception and returns a stack trace.
A cursor from another tenant's export is accepted and returns that tenant's rows.
Clients parse cursors to build their own, coupling to internals that later break.

evidence.locator: §3.1.2 Cursor — result is opaque to the client, passed back as after/before
evidence.note: Opaqueness directly implies servers cannot trust cursor content and clients must round-trip rather than construct cursors.

evidence.locator: Link-header URLs with rel relations; do not guess or construct pagination URLs
evidence.note: Clients must follow server-issued pagination relations; hand-built or foreign cursors are outside the contract and must fail safely.

scenarios.given: a list endpoint with cursor pagination
scenarios.when: truncated, cross-endpoint, and hand-edited cursors are submitted
expect: each is rejected with a documented error or handled per policy, with no crash, no stack-trace disclosure, and no cross-scope data

rules.title: Bind cursors to the query that produced them
rules.statement: A cursor must only be honored against the query that produced it — including filters, sort, direction, and authorization scope. Reuse across a different query must be rejected or explicitly re-scoped per documented policy, never silently return the wrong slice.
why: A cursor encodes a position inside one ordered, filtered set; against another set the same position bytes mean something else entirely.
Silent cross-query acceptance returns confidently wrong data — missing rows with no error — which clients cannot detect.
Scope changes (tenant, permission set) turn a stale cursor into an access-boundary bug when the cursor outlives its authorization context.
applies_when: Cursors are accepted alongside filters, sorts, or scoped authorization.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: A cursor from "status=open" paged against "status=closed" returns open rows labeled as closed.
Changing sort direction mid-traversal silently restarts or scrambles the sequence.
A cursor issued under one tenant's scope is replayed under another.

evidence.locator: ExclusiveStartKey used with the same KeyConditionExpression; Limit scoping
evidence.note: The continuation key is only meaningful against the query that produced it; Boring generalizes the same-query requirement to filters, sorts, direction, and scopes.

scenarios.given: a cursor issued for one filter/sort/scope combination
scenarios.when: it is replayed against a different combination
expect: the request is rejected or re-scoped per documented policy; the wrong slice is never returned silently

rules.title: Terminate correctly on empty and exact-boundary pages
rules.statement: The end of a paginated set must be signaled by the explicit continuation state (absent token, has_more/hasNextPage false) — never inferred from item counts. Empty result sets are valid data, and a page that fills exactly to the boundary must still report whether more data follows.
why: Filtered pages can return zero items while more data remains; treating empty as done truncates the traversal.
A full final page looks identical to a full non-final page by count; only the continuation signal distinguishes them.
Clients that loop "while page is full" request forever or stop one page early depending on which miscount they chose.
applies_when: Any paginated listing exists.
failure_modes: A filtered page returns zero items with a continuation token and the client stops, losing the remaining data.
Forty items at page size twenty report has_more true on page 2, sending the client into a fruitless page 3 loop.
Empty results return an error instead of a valid empty page with correct page info.

evidence.locator: LastEvaluatedKey semantics — non-empty key is a page boundary, not proof of more data; filtered pages may return zero items with a key; absent key ends the set
evidence.note: Directly establishes count-independent termination: the absent key, not the item count, ends traversal.

evidence.locator: List response — has_more false comprises the end of the list
evidence.note: The end signal is the explicit has_more flag on a full or partial page, not the page filling exactly.

evidence.locator: §5.1 PageInfo — startCursor/endCursor null when no results; HasNextPage/HasPreviousPage algorithms over filtered edges
evidence.note: Empty connections null their cursors and compute page flags from the filtered edge set, keeping empty pages valid and terminal states explicit.

scenarios.given: a dataset of exactly two full pages plus a filtered query with an empty first page
scenarios.when: each is traversed to completion
expect: the exact-boundary page reports no further pages and fetching stops
the empty page is valid data with correct page info, and traversal continues while a continuation token is present

rules.title: Enforce documented page-size defaults and maxima server-side
rules.statement: Every paginated endpoint must define a default page size and a maximum page size, enforce them on the server regardless of client input, and handle out-of-range requests (zero, negative, non-numeric, excessive) per documented policy — clamping or rejecting, never allocating unbounded work or returning an undocumented shape.
why: Client-supplied sizes are untrusted; an unenforced limit is a resource-exhaustion vector and a response-shape lottery.
Silent server-side reduction without documentation leaves clients paging against a size they did not ask for.
The right numbers differ per endpoint and dataset, which is why values are a documented decision but enforcement is not optional.
applies_when: Clients can influence page size.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: limit=1000000 materializes a million rows and times out the database.
limit=0 returns the entire table or an undocumented error shape.
The server silently halves oversized pages while Link headers still describe the requested size.

evidence.locator: Parameters — limit 1–100, default 10
evidence.note: Bounds and defaults are part of the pagination contract; Boring requires them documented and enforced without fixing Stripe's numbers as universal.

evidence.locator: per_page maximum 100 with automatic reduction; Link header carries the effective per_page
evidence.note: Demonstrates why the effective size must be explicit: silent reduction confuses clients unless documented and reflected in navigation links.

scenarios.given: the endpoint's documented default and maximum page sizes
scenarios.when: zero, negative, non-numeric, and excessive sizes are requested
expect: each is clamped or rejected per the documented policy and the maximum is never exceeded

rules.title: Keep backward pagination in the same order
rules.statement: Wherever backward traversal (before/last, ending_before) is offered, it must preserve the list's business order — not return pages in reverse — with correct hasPreviousPage/startCursor semantics, so forward-then- backward traversal returns to the same items.
why: Reversing row order on the way back breaks every client that concatenates pages in display order.
The cursor nearest the resume point must sit at the defined edge of the returned page or clients cannot chain pages in either direction.
Offering backward paging with forward-only correctness is worse than not offering it — clients build on the promise.
applies_when: The API supports backward pagination (before/last or equivalent).
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: Backward pages arrive newest-last while forward pages arrive newest-first, scrambling concatenation.
hasPreviousPage stays true on the first page, trapping clients in a backward loop.

evidence.locator: §4.3 Edge order — same ordering for first/after and last/before, not reversed; edge nearest the cursor comes last for before, first for after
evidence.note: Directly requires order preservation across directions; Boring applies the round-trip expectation to any backward-paging API, GraphQL or REST.

evidence.locator: starting_after / ending_before — mutually exclusive cursors over one reverse-chronological order
evidence.note: Both directions address opposite sides of the same ordered list rather than re-sorting it.

scenarios.given: a client mid-list after forward traversal
scenarios.when: it pages backward with before/last and then forward again
expect: items appear in the same business order in both directions and the round trip returns the same items

rules.title: Decide the totals and random-access policy deliberately
rules.statement: Deliberately decide whether the API offers exact totals and random page access (page N of M), and document the choice: exact counts over large or changing datasets are expensive and go stale mid-traversal, while cursor traversal cannot address arbitrary pages.
why: Exact totals such as page 42 of 9,183 need an exact count plus stable addressing; changing datasets invalidate both between requests.
Count queries over large tables are slow and lock-adjacent; approximate or cached counts with disclaimers are often the honest answer.
The mistake is drifting into totals implicitly — exposing a total because the ORM paginator includes one — rather than choosing.
applies_when: List responses could include totals or accept page numbers.
failure_modes: A "total" computed once at page 1 contradicts page 5 after concurrent writes, and the UI shows impossible navigation.
Jump-to-page is offered over keyset traversal by reintroducing offset under the hood without documenting its shift-instability.

evidence.locator: Keyset pages with no total or page numbers; forward-only resumption via ExclusiveStartKey
evidence.note: Demonstrates a production pagination model without totals or random access; Boring treats totals as a deliberate product decision, not a default.

evidence.locator: Link-header relations (next/prev/first/last) as the navigation contract
evidence.note: Shows relation-based navigation as an alternative to client-computed page arithmetic; whether page numbers are offered at all is the documented decision.

scenarios.given: the documented totals and random-access policy
scenarios.when: listing code and responses are reviewed
expect: exposed totals match the documented exactness (exact, approximate with disclaimer, or absent) and page-number access matches the documented mechanism

rules.title: Define cursor lifetime and invalidation
rules.statement: Define how long cursors stay valid and what invalidates them — data retention, sort-key updates, schema or encoding changes, encryption-key rotation — and handle expired cursors per documented policy rather than failing mysteriously.
why: A cursor is a promise about future reads; retention purges, key updates, and re-encodings break the promise silently when no policy exists.
Eternal cursors and expiring cursors are both legitimate; the bug is clients discovering the choice through production failures.
Anchor rows that move or vanish mid-traversal need a defined outcome (miss, repeat, or exclude) instead of an undefined one.
applies_when: Cursors can outlive the state they were issued against.
failure_modes: A week-old bookmarked cursor decodes against a rotated key and returns a 500 with an encoding stack trace.
Retention deletes the anchor row and traversal silently restarts from the head with no signal.

evidence.locator: LastEvaluatedKey as a primary-key position; resumption assumes the key space still exists
evidence.note: Key-position cursors are durable while the key space is; retention and schema changes bound that durability, which Boring requires to be documented.

evidence.locator: §3.1.2 opaque cursors; §4.4 cursor filtering against current edges
evidence.note: Opaque cursors leave lifetime and missing-anchor behavior to the server; Boring requires that server choice to be explicit rather than accidental.

scenarios.given: the documented cursor lifetime and invalidation events
scenarios.when: an expired or invalidated cursor is presented
expect: behavior matches the documented policy (clear error, restart token, or defined resumption) with no crash or silent restart

spec.title: Webhooks
spec.summary: Behavior a webhook consumer must implement to be correct under real delivery semantics: at-least-once delivery, no ordering guarantees, retries, replay, and provider evolution.
applies_when: The application exposes an HTTP endpoint that receives events (webhooks, callbacks, notifications) from a provider.
does_not_apply_when: The application only sends webhooks to others (see provider-side concerns in a future spec).
Events are consumed via polling or a message queue without HTTP delivery semantics.

rules.title: Process deliveries idempotently
rules.statement: Webhook processing must be safe to repeat. Receiving the same delivery — or an equivalent event for the same object and action — more than once must not duplicate business side effects.
why: Providers deliver at-least-once; retries after timeouts and manual redelivery both produce duplicates.
Some providers generate two distinct event objects for one underlying occurrence, so deduplication must also work at the business-object level.
HTTP retries are only safe for idempotent operations (RFC 9110 §9.2.2).
applies_when: The application consumes webhook or event deliveries from any provider.
failure_modes: A retried payment event creates a second order or a second charge.
The same transactional email is sent twice.
A handler that partially succeeded before failing duplicates its effects when retried.

evidence.locator: Duplicates; Event ordering; Retries; Signatures
evidence.note: Boring derives this framework-neutral requirement from the cited STRIPE-WEBHOOK-DOCS behavior and the failure mode; the source is not being presented as a universal vendor-independent mandate.

scenarios.when: the exact same delivery arrives again
expect: business side effects are not duplicated
the delivery is still acknowledged with a 2xx response

scenarios.given: two distinct event objects describing one underlying occurrence
scenarios.when: both are processed
expect: the business effect (order, email, state change) happens exactly once

rules.title: Verify sender authenticity and fail closed
rules.statement: Deliveries must be authenticated using the provider's signature scheme — typically an HMAC over the raw request body with a shared secret. Requests with missing, malformed, or invalid signatures must be rejected without processing, and comparisons must be constant-time.
why: Webhook endpoint URLs are reachable by anyone on the internet; without signature verification, anyone can forge events.
Provider guidance specifies HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body (Stripe `v1` scheme; GitHub `X-Hub-Signature-256`).
Timing-safe comparison is explicitly recommended by providers.
applies_when: The provider offers a signature or authentication scheme for deliveries.
exceptions: Providers that offer no signature scheme require a different authenticating channel (e.g., verifying via a follow-up authenticated API call).
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: A forged event triggers a state change (e.g., "payment succeeded" for a payment that never happened).
The signature is checked against the parsed/re-serialized body instead of the raw bytes and fails or passes incorrectly.
Non-constant-time comparison leaks signature bytes.

rules.title: Enforce replay windows when the scheme embeds a timestamp
rules.statement: When the provider's signature scheme includes a delivery timestamp, verification should reject deliveries whose timestamp is older than a documented tolerance window; verifying the HMAC alone is not replay protection.

Stripe's timestamp is part of the signed payload and its libraries use a default tolerance of five minutes.

exceptions: Schemes without timestamps need application-level deduplication by delivery/event ID instead.
does_not_apply_when: The feature, transport, or protocol described in applies_when is not used; this rule is not a substitute for a different contract.
failure_modes: An old but correctly signed delivery is accepted and re-triggers processing (replay attack).

rules.statement: Return a 2xx response promptly — before slow or complex logic — and perform processing asynchronously (e.g., via a queue). Long synchronous processing risks timeouts, which providers treat as failed delivery and then retry.
why: GitHub terminates connections and marks the delivery failed if no 2xx arrives within 10 seconds.
Stripe recommends returning a 2xx before any logic that could cause a timeout, and processing via asynchronous queues.

rules.statement: A 2xx response tells the provider to stop retrying. Return 2xx only once the delivery is durably accepted (e.g., persisted to a queue or store); a crash between acknowledging and processing must not lose the event.
why: Providers define success as any 2xx (and treat redirects as failures); no further retry will follow a 2xx.

sources.title: HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110)
sources.notes: Idempotent methods (§9.2.2) and 2xx success semantics (§15.3) anchor the webhook delivery rules.

sources.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format (RFC 8259)
sources.notes: Numbers that cannot be represented (NaN, Infinity) are not permitted (§6); object member names SHOULD be unique (§4).

sources.title: Best Current Practices for JSON Web Tokens (RFC 8725)
sources.notes: Algorithm and claim validation requirements for JWT-based sessions.

sources.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps (RFC 3339)
sources.notes: Timestamp grammar (§5.6): Z denotes UTC offset zero (§2); -00:00 signals unknown local offset (§4.3); time-second may be 60 at leap seconds (§5.6, §5.7); a space may replace T by NOTE.

sources.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (RFC 5321)
sources.notes: Local-part limit 64 octets (§4.5.3.1.1), path limit 256 octets (§4.5.3.1.3), address literals (§4.1.3); local-part case sensitivity (§2.4) and its interoperability warning.

sources.title: Internet Message Format (RFC 5322)
sources.notes: dot-atom syntax (§3.2.3), quoted-string local parts and display names (§3.4.1).

sources.title: SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email (SMTPUTF8) (RFC 6531)
sources.notes: Unicode local parts require end-to-end SMTPUTF8 support (§3.2, §3.4).

sources.title: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework (RFC 5890)
sources.notes: A-labels with xn-- prefix (§2.3.2.1); the 63-octet DNS limit applies to A-labels (§2.3.1).

sources.title: Unicode Normalization Forms (UAX
sources.notes: NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD (§1.2); canonical equivalence (§1.1); normalization not closed under concatenation (§1.4).

sources.title: Unicode Text Segmentation (UAX
sources.notes: Extended grapheme clusters approximate user-perceived characters (§3); emoji ZWJ sequences are single grapheme clusters (GB11); regional indicator pairs (GB12/GB13).

sources.title: Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX
sources.notes: Ordering of mixed-direction text; isolates as the scoping mechanism.

sources.title: Unicode Security Mechanisms (UTS
sources.notes: Confusable detection via skeleton comparison (§4); mixed-script detection (§5.1); identifier restrictions, including ZWJ/ZWNJ (§3.1, §7).

sources.title: Unicode Security Considerations (UTS
sources.notes: Invisible characters affecting rendering (§2.4); non-visual bypasses when components treat text as identical after transformation (§3); visual spoofing via confusables (§2). Note: the canonical tr36 URL now serves a stabilization notice; the maintained text is at tr36-15.html.

sources.title: Unicode IDNA Compatibility Processing (UTS
sources.notes: Compatibility mapping for IDNA2008 (§2); transitional vs nontransitional processing differs only on the four Deviation characters (§1.3.2).

sources.title: The Unicode Standard (core specification)
sources.notes: Case folding for caseless matching; code point semantics.

sources.title: Unicode Common Locale Data Repository (CLDR)
sources.notes: Locale conventions for number formatting and parsing (decimal separators, grouping).

sources.title: IANA Time Zone Database
sources.notes: History and rules of local time for worldwide locations; "updated periodically to reflect changes made by political bodies to time zone boundaries, UTC offsets, and daylight-saving rules"; "current predictions will be incorrect after future governments change the rules".

sources.title: HTML Standard (WHATWG)
sources.notes: input type=email validation (§4.10.5.1.5): a willful violation of RFC 5322 with a defined regex that accepts single-label domains.

sources.title: URL Standard (WHATWG)
sources.notes: Canonical URL parsing model, including scheme-relative and embedded-credential forms.

sources.title: GraphQL Cursor Connections Specification
sources.notes: Opaque per-edge cursors (§3.1.2); forward arguments first/after (§4.1) and backward arguments last/before (§4.2); edge order must be consistent and not reversed for backward pagination (§4.3); cursor-filtering and first/last slicing algorithm (§4.4); PageInfo hasNextPage/hasPreviousPage/startCursor/ endCursor semantics (§5.1).

sources.title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) 5.0.0
sources.notes: Released 30 May 2025. V6 Authentication (credential reset, notifications 6.3.7/6.3.8/6.4.3), V7 Session Management (timeouts 7.3.1/7.3.2, session termination 7.4.x, user session control 7.5.2), V9 Self-contained Tokens.

sources.title: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet
sources.notes: Primary source for the password-reset spec: enumeration resistance, token generation/expiry/single-use/storage, throttling, notifications, session invalidation, password policy on reset.

sources.title: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
sources.notes: Generic error messages, password length/composition/blocklist guidance, re-authentication for sensitive features.

sources.title: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet
sources.notes: Primary source for the sessions spec: ≥64-bit entropy, cookie attributes, renewal on authentication and privilege change, server-side logout, timeout ranges (idle 15-30 min low-risk / 2-5 min high-value; absolute 4-8 h), no URL-based identifiers, user session control.

sources.title: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.notes: SameSite's role as a defense layer complementary to CSRF countermeasures.

sources.title: OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
sources.notes: Primary source for the file-uploads spec: extension allowlists, content-vs-declared-type warnings, validation after decoding, randomized storage names ("essential"), protected storage locations, read access control "a must", size limits, zip bombs, archive handling, AV/sandbox advice. Note: it does not cover serving headers (Content-Disposition, nosniff) or image decompression bombs — those carry MDN citations or field-knowledge flags.

sources.title: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet
sources.notes: Validate all potentially untrusted input as early as possible; allowlist over denylist; canonical encoding across text; free-form Unicode text (links UAX #15). Note: "validation after decoding" wording lives in the File Upload sheet, not here.

sources.title: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet
sources.notes: Salted, slow hashing (Argon2id, bcrypt, PBKDF2), work factors — applied in Boring to reset-token storage.

sources.title: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG)
sources.notes: Standard test taxonomy; referenced for unvalidated redirect testing and general verification approaches.

sources.title: OWASP Denial of Service Cheat Sheet
sources.notes: Guidance to analyze application DoS surfaces, limit input-driven resource allocation, and bound expensive processing such as image resizing.

sources.title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B (Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management), Revision 4
sources.notes: Final Rev 4 (July 2025) supersedes 800-63B (Rev 3: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html). Password minimums (15 single-factor / 8 with MFA), SHOULD allow ≥64 chars and all printing ASCII/Unicode with each code point counted as one character, SHALL NOT composition rules, SHALL blocklist breached passwords, SHALL rate-limit failed attempts. Rev 3 retained for readers on the earlier revision.

sources.title: Stripe Webhooks documentation
sources.notes: At-least-once delivery and duplicates; no ordering guarantee ("Don't use created to determine event order"); retries up to three days with exponential backoff; 2xx = delivered, redirects are failures; Stripe- Signature scheme (t= timestamp, v1 HMAC-SHA256, constant-time comparison); 5-minute default replay tolerance; 2xx-before-logic best practice; secret rolling with previous secret active up to 24 hours.

sources.title: Stripe Idempotent Requests documentation
sources.notes: Request-side idempotency mechanics ("safely retrying requests without accidentally performing the same operation twice") — supporting evidence for consumer-side idempotency design.

sources.title: GitHub — Best practices for using webhooks
sources.notes: 2xx within 10 seconds or the delivery fails; X-GitHub-Delivery identifies deliveries (same value on manual redelivery); redeliver missed webhooks after downtime; async queue processing.

sources.title: GitHub — Validating webhook deliveries
sources.notes: X-Hub-Signature-256 (HMAC-SHA256, sha256= prefix) validation guidance.

sources.title: MDN — Content-Disposition header
sources.notes: attachment disposition semantics for serving user content safely.

sources.title: MDN — X-Content-Type-Options header (nosniff)
sources.notes: nosniff semantics preventing MIME-type sniffing of served content.

sources.title: PostgreSQL documentation — LIMIT/OFFSET and ORDER BY
sources.notes: LIMIT/OFFSET (§7.6) requires an ORDER BY constraining rows into a unique order, otherwise subsets are unpredictable and different LIMIT/OFFSET values give inconsistent results; large OFFSET still computes skipped rows and may be inefficient. ORDER BY (§7.5) guarantees order only when explicitly chosen.

sources.title: Stripe API pagination documentation
sources.notes: Cursor pagination via limit (1–100, default 10) with mutually exclusive starting_after/ending_before object-ID cursors in reverse chronological order; list responses carry data plus has_more and url.

sources.title: GitHub REST API — Using pagination
sources.notes: Page (page/per_page) and cursor (before/after) query parameters with server-issued Link-header URLs (rel next/prev/first/last); per_page maximum 100 with silent reduction above the max; clients must follow Link relations rather than constructing URLs.

sources.title: DynamoDB — Paginating table query results
sources.notes: Keyset pagination via LastEvaluatedKey/ExclusiveStartKey with the same KeyConditionExpression and Limit; pages are 1 MB or less; a non-empty LastEvaluatedKey marks a page boundary, not proof of more data, and filtered pages can return zero items with a continuation key; absence of the key ends the set.

sources.title: Big List of Naughty Strings
sources.notes: "A list of strings which have a high probability of causing issues when used as user-input data." Used to discover categories and find omissions; Boring's datasets are original representations, not imports.

sources.title: Web Platform Tests
sources.notes: Cross-browser test suite for the Web platform stack (WHATWG, W3C specs) — reference for how specifications become executable tests.
